title: Cash, positions and equity
objectives: Track cash, holdings and equity correctly through every trade.
Show that a fill changes equity only by its cost.

screens.title: A five-day ledger
screens.prose: A £10,000 account trades one share whose close starts at £50.00. Each row is one day: the fill happens during the day, then the books are marked at the close. **Equity** is what the account is worth: the cash plus the shares at that close.
screens.question: Fill in the cash and the equity at the end of days 1 and 2.

hints.text: The buy pays 100 × £50.10 plus the £1 fee out of cash.

feedback.correct: Cash moves only when we trade; equity moves every day with the close.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cash falls by the shares' price plus the fee; equity is cash plus shares times the close.

explain.text: The buy turned £5,011 of cash into 100 shares and a £1 fee. On day 2 nothing traded, so cash stayed at £4,989, and equity fell £60 with the close. Marking the shares at each close is **marking to market**.

screens.title: Where the money went
screens.prose: Day 1 again, just after the fill: cash £4,989 and 100 shares. Slide the day's close and watch equity.
screens.question: At what close is equity back to exactly £10,000?

feedback.correct: £50.11: the fill price plus 1p a share for the fee.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the close where cash plus 100 shares makes £10,000.

byKey.fill: At the fill price, £50.10, equity is £9,999: the £1 fee is still missing.
byKey.start: At £50.00 equity is £9,989. The fill was 10p above that, and the fee is on top.

explain.text: Equity is £10,000 at a close of £50.11. The fill moved £5,010 from cash into shares worth £5,010, and the £1 fee was the only real loss. Every pound above £50.11 is market move, not accounting.

screens.title: What a fill does to equity
screens.prose: Mark the shares at the fill price itself, the instant after the day-1 buy of 100 at £50.10 with a £1 fee. Before the fill: £10,000 cash, no shares.
screens.question: By how much does equity change at the moment of the fill, in £?

widget.label: Change in equity (£)
widget.placeholder: a negative number for a fall
widget.accept: −£1: only the fee leaves the account.

feedback.correct: Equity falls by the fee and nothing else.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute equity after the fill at £50.10 and compare it with £10,000.

byKey.cash: That is the change in cash. The £5,010 did not vanish: it became 100 shares worth £5,010.
byKey.zero: The shares are worth what was paid, but the £1 fee is gone.

explain.text: At the fill price, the shares are worth exactly the cash paid for them, so the fill moves value between two pockets. Only the cost leaves: equity goes from £10,000 to £9,999. Any change after that comes from the close moving away from the fill.

screens.title: Adding, then selling out
screens.prose: Days 3 and 4. Day 3 buys 50 more at £49.70; day 4 sells all 150 at £50.60. Each trade pays a £1 fee. Edge case: after day 4 the account holds exactly 0 shares.
screens.question: Fill in cash, shares and equity for days 3 and 4.

hints.text: A sale adds the proceeds to cash, then subtracts the fee.
Day 3 equity 2,503 + 150 × 50.20 = 10,033. Day 4 cash 10,092, 0 shares, equity 10,092.

feedback.correct: Flat after day 4: equity is all cash, £10,092.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A buy spends price × shares plus the fee; a sale receives price × shares minus the fee.

explain.text: With 0 shares, equity is the cash and the close no longer matters: day 4's close of £50.90 adds nothing. The round trip made £92 after three £1 fees. A position closed to exactly 0 must leave no leftover shares, which the code tests check.

screens.title: A short sale
screens.prose: Day 5: from flat, sell 80 shares we do not own at £51.00, with a £1 fee. This is a **short**: cash goes up, shares go negative, and we owe the shares back.
screens.question: Fill in cash, shares and equity at the end of day 5.

hints.text: The sale brings in 80 × £51.00, less the fee.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A short sale adds the proceeds to cash, and the negative shares are marked at the close.

explain.text: The £4,080 in cash is not profit: we owe 80 shares, worth −£4,104 at the close. Equity fell £25: the £1 fee plus 80 × 30p as the price rose against the short. The same formula, cash plus shares times price, works with negative shares.

screens.title: A day with no trade
screens.prose: Day 6: no trade. The account is short 80 shares, and the close falls from £51.30 to £50.80. Cash does not move.
screens.question: By how much does equity change on day 6, in £?

widget.label: Change in equity (£)
widget.placeholder: a negative number for a fall

hints.text: With no trade, only shares × the price change moves equity.
The price change is −£0.50, and shares are −80.

feedback.correct: A falling price makes a short £40 richer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the shares held by the change in close.

byKey.sign: You treated the short as a long. With −80 shares, a 50p fall is a gain: −80 × −0.50 = +40.
byKey.cash: Cash did not move, but the shares owed got cheaper, so equity did.

explain.text: On a day with no trade, the change in equity is shares held times the change in close: $-80 \times (-0.50) = +40$. Equity goes from £10,067 to £10,107. That is the whole of a day's P&L.

screens.title: The portfolio in code
screens.prose: Write the portfolio the engine fills. `fill(qty, price, cost)` buys `qty` shares at `price` (a sale when `qty` is negative) and pays `cost`. A zero quantity is no trade: nothing changes, not even the cost. `equity(price)` marks the shares at `price`.
screens.question: Complete the class `Portfolio`.

widget.prelude:
import random

DAYS = [(100, 50.10, 1.0, 50.40), (0, 0.0, 0.0, 49.80), (50, 49.70, 1.0, 50.20),
        (-150, 50.60, 1.0, 50.90), (-80, 51.00, 1.0, 51.30)]

def run_ledger(cls):
    """The lesson's five days on a 10,000 account: (qty, fill price, cost, close) each day."""
    p = cls(10_000)
    out = []
    for qty, price, cost, close in DAYS:
        p.fill(qty, price, cost)
        out.append(round(p.equity(close), 2))
    return out

def conservation(cls, n=200, seed=7):
    """200 random fills: equity at the fill price must fall by exactly the cost."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    p = cls(100_000)
    worst = 0.0
    for _ in range(n):
        qty = rng.randint(-500, 500)
        price = round(rng.uniform(20, 80), 2)
        cost = round(rng.uniform(0, 5), 2) if qty else 0.0
        before = p.equity(price)
        p.fill(qty, price, cost)
        worst = max(worst, abs((before - p.equity(price)) - cost))
    return worst < 1e-9
widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: the lesson's five-day ledger (`run_ledger`, equities to 2 places), a new account, a short and its cover, a zero-quantity fill, the default cost of 0, and `conservation`: 200 random fills from `random.Random(7)`, where equity at the fill price must fall by exactly the cost, to 1e-9. Both helpers are already defined. Pure Python: nothing to load.

hints.text: A buy spends `qty * price`; a sale has negative `qty`, so the same line raises cash.
Start `fill` with `if qty == 0: return`, and return `self.cash + self.shares * price` from `equity`.

feedback.correct: The ledger matches, and 200 random fills each cost exactly their fee.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. One line moves cash by `qty * price + cost`; one moves shares by `qty`.

byKey.test-5: A zero-quantity fill changed the account. No trade means no fee.
byKey.test-7: Some fill changed equity by more or less than its cost. Check the sign: a sale adds `-qty * price` to cash.

explain.text: One signed line handles buys, sales, shorts and covers: `cash -= qty * price + cost`. The conservation test checks the identity behind the whole lesson on 200 fills at once. Lesson 5's engine calls this `fill` for every order.

screens.title: Marking at the wrong price
screens.prose: Back to day 1: buy 100 at £50.10 with a £1 fee, close £50.40. Four colleagues report the day's closing equity.
screens.question: Which figure is right?

options.why: You marked the shares at the fill price. The day ends at the close, £50.40, so the shares are worth £5,040.
You charged the £1 fee twice: once in cash and once more off equity. Cash already paid it.
You left out the £1 fee. Cash paid £5,011, not £5,010.

hints.text: Equity at the end of the day uses the close.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take cash after the fee, then mark the shares at the close.

byKey.fillpx: That marks at the fill price, which is right only at the instant of the fill. Mark-to-market uses the close.
byKey.twice: The fee comes out of cash once. Subtracting it again from equity counts it twice.

explain.text: The fill price sets the cash; the close sets the value of the shares. Mixing them up makes every day's P&L wrong by the gap between fill and close. Charging the fee in two places makes each trade £1 dearer than it was.

screens.title: Why a fill costs only its cost
screens.prose: Every row you filled obeyed one identity: equity is cash plus shares times price, $E = C + S\,p$. A fill of $q$ shares at $p$ with cost $c$ sets $C' = C - qp - c$ and $S' = S + q$. Show what it does to equity at that same price.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $E = C + S\,p$: equity before the fill, marked at the fill price
$E' = C' + S'\,p$: equity after the fill, at the same price
$E' = (C - qp - c) + (S + q)\,p$: substitute the new cash and shares
$E' = C + Sp - c$: the $-qp$ and $+qp$ cancel
$E' = E - c$: the first two terms are $E$

hints.text: Start from the two definitions of equity, before and after.
a and b, then c, d, e.

feedback.correct: A fill changes equity by $-c$ and nothing else.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write both equities, substitute, then cancel.

byKey.e: $E' = E - c$ is the conclusion. It comes after the $qp$ terms cancel.

explain.text: The $qp$ paid in cash reappears as $q$ shares worth $p$ each, so they cancel. What is left is $E' = E - c$, for buys and sales, longs and shorts alike. Your `conservation` test checks this line on 200 fills.

screens.title: Reconciling with the broker
screens.prose: After a year of paper trading, the broker's statement shows £1,000,000 less £61,240 of commissions over 3,062 trades. The engine's equity curve is smooth and matches the broker's in shape, but ends £61,240 higher. Its Sharpe ratio and drawdown look entirely plausible.
screens.question: What is the likeliest bug, and what would have caught it?

options.text: The engine's `fill` never subtracts the cost; a daily reconciliation of cash against the broker catches it
A look-ahead leak; a Sharpe above 2 would have flagged it
options.why: A missing fee adds a steady £20 per trade, which looks like a slightly better strategy. The Sharpe stays ordinary, so no metric flags it.

options.text: Marking at the fill price; the drawdown would have shown it
options.why: That bug moves each day's P&L up or down by the fill-to-close gap. It would not add up to exactly the commission total.
The gap equals the commission total to the pound. The engine is the one leaving something out.

hints.text: The gap is exactly the total commission.
Costs are missing from cash. Only comparing cash and shares with an outside record finds that.

feedback.correct: Reconcile cash and shares, not just the curve's shape.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the gap equals.

explain.text: A dropped cost makes every trade £20 too profitable, a smooth bias that no Sharpe or drawdown check can see. Desks reconcile cash and positions against the broker every day for this reason. In a backtest, the `conservation` test plays the broker's part.

ideas: Equity is cash plus shares times price, marked to market at every close.
A fill moves value between cash and shares; at the fill price it changes equity only by its cost.
One signed line covers buys, sales, shorts and covers; a zero order changes nothing; a flat account's equity is its cash.

formula.name: Equity
formula.tex: E = C + S\,p, \qquad \text{fill: } C' = C - qp - c,\; S' = S + q \;\Rightarrow\; E' = E - c
formula.note: Mark at the close for the day's equity; at the fill price only to check the identity.

summary.trap: Marking at the fill price, or charging the cost twice, gives a smooth, wrong equity curve that no metric catches.

quiz.question: What is the cash afterwards, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cash falls by 200 × £25.05 and by the fee.

quiz.prose: A flat account with £20,000 cash sells short 100 shares at £40.00 with a £2 fee.
quiz.question: What happens at the moment of the fill?

options.text: Cash rises to £23,998, shares go to −100, and equity at £40 falls to £19,998

options.why: You counted the proceeds as profit. The account owes 100 shares, worth −£4,000, which cancel them.

options.text: Cash falls by £4,002, because shares were traded
options.why: A sale, short or not, brings cash in. Cash falls only on a buy.

feedback.correct: Proceeds in, negative shares, equity down by the fee.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply cash − qp − c with q = −100.

explain.text: With $q = -100$: cash becomes 20,000 + 4,000 − 2 = 23,998 and shares −100. Equity at £40 is 23,998 − 4,000 = 19,998: down by the fee, as for any fill.

quiz.prose: An account is short 80 shares. On a day with no trade the close moves from £51.30 to £50.80.
quiz.question: How does equity change, in £?

widget.placeholder: a negative number for a fall

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the shares held by the change in price.
